The challenge in diagnosing skin cancer lies in the similarity between its various forms, resulting in difficulties when distinguishing them.  To address this issue, a novel deep learning-based approach, referred to as the Skin Cancer Classification Network (SKCCNet), has been proposed.  SKCCNet comprises multiple interconnected neural networks that generate unique feature representations for each type of skin cancer. SKCCNet's superior performance can be attributed to its innovative network design and the incorporation of spatial attention mechanisms that enhance the visibility of important image regions.  The SKCCNet approach and its publicly available code offer valuable insights for the accurate skin cancer classification. Our research utilizes the MutFlow algorithm, a novel method that analyzes large-scale genetic data to determine the transmission dynamics of viral mutations. The algorithm, based on a Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis, identifies the probability of each possible transmission route among observed mutations in viral sequences.
By applying MutFlow to a dataset of over 31,000 SARS-CoV-2 sequences from the time period of March to May 2020, we mapped the viral mutation tree and quantified the probability of transmission between viral variants. Our analysis revealed that SARS-CoV-2 mutations are primarily the result of high mutation rates within viral replication, and transmission occurs through recombination rather than direct contact.
The results indicate that specific combinations of mutations, such as L452, and R521M, R453C, and R453C, have a high probability of transmission between them. Our findings also suggest that these transmission pathways may occur through a common intermediate viral variant.

An investigation of the early spread of Covid-19 in different countries reveals that the virus can exhibit a distinctive pattern of growth during its initial stages in each location. This initial growth can be modelled using a modified version of the SIR model, which takes into consideration the limited resources available to each individual who contracts the virus. As the virus spreads, the available resources become depleted, leading to a sudden drop in cases, which can be seen as a "bump" in growth patterns on graphs of cases over time, hence the term Covid-Bump. Under this model, the early growth of cases can be accurately represented by a power law growth pattern, similar to that observed in the early stages of the Zika virus and Ebola disease. An analysis of cases in the United States for the period from March 29 to May 18, 2020, confirms the applicability of this model to real-world data. However, existing deep learning models based on Bayesian methods face significant computational challenges due to their high inference time and large memory requirements.  A key factor contributing to these challenges is the need to calculate the posterior distribution of model parameters, a time-consuming process that is often approximated by sampling methods such as Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics or Nesterov-Polyak Gradient descent.  In this paper, we propose a new, efficient approach to Bayesian inference for deep learning models that leverages the natural gradient of the posterior distribution to directly update model parameters, thus eliminating the need for sampling.  Our proposed method, Langevin Gradient Descent, is computationally more efficient and memory-friendly than existing sampling-based methods, and can be integrated into various deep learning models, including neural networks and convolutional neural networks.  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable performance to existing sampling-based methods while providing a significant reduction in computational cost and memory requirements.  Moreover, our approach allows for the direct application of gradient descent to the log-posterior, thus enabling the use of traditional deep learning optimizers, and we show that this characteristic is particularly beneficial in the context of uncertainty prediction.  Our findings suggest that this property can be exploited to develop more efficient uncertainty prediction methods.  Finally, we propose a new, gradient-based uncertainty prediction method, Langevin Gradient Descent Uncertainty Prediction, that achieves faster inference times than existing methods while providing comparable accuracy.  Moreover, we show that this method is more robust to hyperparameter choices than existing methods.  Our work provides a new, efficient approach to deep learning models based on Bayesian inference and opens up new opportunities for the development of more efficient deep learning models.
